lead: A beam that is safe against collapse can still sag enough to crack the partitions under it, or crack enough to let water reach its bars. The limit state of serviceability checks the beam under the loads that actually act, the service loads, with a load factor of 1.0. IS 456 controls deflection mainly by a span to depth rule and controls cracking mainly by detailing rules on bar spacing and cover, with a crack-width formula for cases that need a number.
prereq: You need the designed beams of singly reinforced beams; the cracked-section stresses behind the crack-width formula are in cracking moment and transformed sections.

blocks.text: Deflection grows with time: the immediate (short-term) sag under load is followed by creep of the concrete under the sustained load and by shrinkage as it dries, which together can double or triple it. IS 456 sets two limits for beams and slabs:

head: What is limited
Limit
rows: Final deflection, including creep, shrinkage and temperature, measured from the as-cast level
Deflection that happens after partitions and finishes are built, including creep and shrinkage
span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is less

blocks.text: L/350 equals 20 mm at a span of 7 m, so the 20 mm cap governs only for spans longer than 7 m.

sections.h3: The span to effective depth rule

blocks.text: For spans up to 10 m, a beam that satisfies the span/depth rule is taken to meet both limits without computing deflection:

blocks.where: (L/d)basic = 7 for a cantilever, 20 for a simply supported span and 26 for a continuous span; k<sub>t</sub> is the modification factor for tension steel (IS 456 Fig. 4), k<sub>c</sub> for compression steel (Fig. 5) and k<sub>f</sub> for flanged beams (Fig. 6). For spans over 10 m the basic value is multiplied by 10/span, except for cantilevers, which need a deflection calculation.

blocks.text: k<sub>t</sub> depends on the steel percentage p<sub>t</sub> and on the service stress in the steel, f<sub>s</sub> = 0.58 f<sub>y</sub> × (A<sub>st</sub> required/A<sub>st</sub> provided). It is largest, up to 2.0, for lightly reinforced beams: a low p<sub>t</sub> gives a shallow cracked neutral axis and a stiffer section for the same steel stress. It falls as p<sub>t</sub> or f<sub>s</sub> rises. Many designers use the curve fit k<sub>t</sub> = 1/[0.225 + 0.00322 f<sub>s</sub> + 0.625 log₁₀ p<sub>t</sub>] ≤ 2 in place of reading Fig. 4; in an exam, read the chart. k<sub>c</sub> grows from 1.0 with the compression steel percentage p<sub>c</sub> to 1.5 at p<sub>c</sub> = 3 % (close to k<sub>c</sub> = 1 + p<sub>c</sub>/(3 + p<sub>c</sub>)). For flanged beams k<sub>f</sub> is 0.8 when b<sub>w</sub>/b<sub>f</sub> ≤ 0.3 and rises linearly to 1.0 at b<sub>w</sub>/b<sub>f</sub> = 1, and p<sub>t</sub> is then worked out on b<sub>f</sub> d.
If the check fails, more depth helps most, because L/d and fs fall together; extra tension steel or compression steel also helps.

Cracks in a beam cannot be avoided, because concrete cracks at a tensile stress of only 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub>. The aim is many fine cracks instead of a few wide ones. IS 456 (clause 35.3.2) limits the surface crack width to 0.3 mm in general, 0.2 mm where the member is exposed to weather, moisture or soil, and 0.1 mm in a severe environment. In most beams the limit is met by detailing alone:

items: The clear distance between tension bars may not exceed the values of Table 15: 300 mm for Fe250, 180 mm for Fe415 and 150 mm for Fe500 (no moment redistribution).
Beams deeper than 750 mm get side face steel of 0.1 % of the web area, split between the two faces at not more than 300 mm or the web thickness.
Nominal cover by exposure (Table 16): 20 mm mild, 30 mm moderate, 45 mm severe, 50 mm very severe, 75 mm extreme.
Several smaller bars control cracks better than a few large bars of the same area.

blocks.text: w<sub>cr</sub> = 3 a<sub>cr</sub> ε<sub>m</sub> / [1 + 2 (a<sub>cr</sub> − C<sub>min</sub>)/(D − x)]     ε<sub>m</sub> = ε<sub>1</sub> − b (D − x)(a − x) / [3 E<sub>s</sub> A<sub>st</sub> (d − x)]
blocks.where: IS 456 Annex F. a<sub>cr</sub> is the distance from the point considered to the surface of the nearest bar; C<sub>min</sub> the clear cover to the main bars; x the depth of the cracked neutral axis; a the depth of the point considered (a = D at the soffit); ε<sub>1</sub> the strain there from the cracked section; the second term of ε<sub>m</sub> is the stiffening of the concrete between cracks.

examples.question: A roof beam 250 mm wide and 450 mm deep (d = 400 mm) spans 9 m, simply supported, and carries M<sub>u</sub> = 125 kN·m. M25, Fe415. The design needs A<sub>st</sub> = 1048 mm²; 4 bars of 20 mm (1257 mm²) are provided. Check deflection by the span/depth rule, and if it fails, test 2 bars of 16 mm at the top and a 500 mm deep beam (d = 450 mm, A<sub>st</sub> required 885 mm²).
steps: Actual L/d = 9000/400 = 22.5. The span is under 10 m, so (L/d)basic = 20.
Allowed L/d = 20 × 1.07 = 21.4 < 22.5: the beam fails the deflection check.
examples.answer: With d = 400 mm the beam fails (22.5 against 21.4); 2 bars of 16 mm at the top bring the limit to 24.0, and a 500 mm deep beam to 25.0 against 20.0.

examples.question: The beam of the first singly reinforced example (230 × 450 mm, 3 bars of 20 mm, C<sub>min</sub> = 38 mm to the main bars, d = 402 mm, M25) carries a service moment of 75 kN·m. Find the crack width at the bottom corner, taking m = 280/(3σcbc) = 10.98 for M25 (σ<sub>cbc</sub> = 8.5 N/mm²).
steps: Bar centres are 48 mm from the side and the soffit, so at the corner a<sub>cr</sub> = √(48² + 48²) − 10 = 57.9 mm.
Detailing check: clear spacing 47 mm, far less than 180 mm for Fe415.
examples.answer: w<sub>cr</sub> = 0.18 mm at the corner, inside the 0.3 mm general limit and the 0.2 mm limit for exposed members.

traps: Using factored loads in a serviceability check. Service loads have a load factor of 1.0, and f<sub>s</sub> is 0.58 f<sub>y</sub>, not 0.87 f<sub>y</sub>.
Comparing the after-partition deflection with span/250. The limit is span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is less.
Forgetting the 10/span reduction for spans over 10 m: at 12 m the basic simply supported value is 20 × 10/12 = 16.7.
Reading k<sub>t</sub> as rising with steel. k<sub>t</sub> falls as p<sub>t</sub> and f<sub>s</sub> rise; a heavily reinforced beam is allowed a smaller L/d.
Thinking a deeper cover always makes narrower cracks. More cover protects the bar, but a<sub>cr</sub> grows with it and so does the surface crack width; the code accepts this for durability.

quiz.q: State the basic span/effective depth ratios of IS 456 for beams up to 10 m.
What crack widths does IS 456 allow?
quiz.a: 0.3 mm in general, 0.2 mm for members exposed to weather, moisture or soil, and 0.1 mm in a particularly aggressive environment.

quiz.q: Why is the after-partition limit stricter than span/250?
quiz.a: Brick partitions and finishes crack under much smaller movements than the beam can take; only the part of the deflection that happens after they are built can damage them, and it is limited to span/350 or 20 mm.

quiz.q: Why does providing more steel than required raise k<sub>t</sub>?
quiz.a: f<sub>s</sub> = 0.58 f<sub>y</sub> × A<sub>st,req</sub>/A<sub>st,prov</sub> falls, and a lower service steel stress means smaller curvature and deflection, so a larger span/depth is allowed.

quiz.q: A continuous beam spans 12 m with d = 600 mm and k<sub>t</sub> = 1.1. Does it pass?
quiz.a: Basic value 26 × 10/12 = 21.7. Allowed 21.7 × 1.1 = 23.8. Actual 12 000/600 = 20.0. It passes.

quiz.q: In worked example 1, which remedy would you choose and why?
quiz.a: The 500 mm deep beam: it passes with the larger margin (20.0 against 25.0), needs less tension steel (885 against 1048 mm²) and reduces crack widths. The top bars are the answer only if the depth is fixed.

quiz.q: Why is the corner the critical point in worked example 2?
quiz.a: The crack width grows with a<sub>cr</sub>, the distance to the nearest bar surface; the corner is farther from a bar (57.9 mm) than the soffit midway between bars (48.5 mm), so its crack is widest.

beyond: Not for the exam. Long spans, cantilevers and transfer girders get a direct deflection calculation (IS 456 Annex C), and long floors also a footfall vibration check. Search for floor vibration serviceability.

figure.caption: The tension-steel factor k<sub>t</sub> falls as the steel percentage and the service stress rise. The 9 m roof beam with d = 400 mm sits at k<sub>t</sub> = 1.07 and fails; deepening it to d = 450 mm lowers both p<sub>t</sub> and f<sub>s</sub> and lifts k<sub>t</sub> to 1.25.
